questions.q: Define self-efficacy and state the theorist associated with its origin. How does it differ from self-esteem in terms of scope (global vs. domain-specific)?
questions.a: Self-efficacy is the belief in one's capability to organize and execute actions required to manage prospective situations; it was proposed by Albert Bandura. Self-efficacy is domain-specific (e.g., "I can solve math problems"), whereas self-esteem is a global evaluation of self-worth ("I am a worthwhile person"). A wrong answer that defines self-efficacy as "confidence" without mentioning Bandura or domain-specificity reveals confusion between the two constructs and lack of theoretical grounding.

questions.q: A student says: "I have high self-efficacy for public speaking because I got an A in English last year." Identify the source of self-efficacy information this student is using (Bandura's four sources) and explain why this particular source is the most powerful.
questions.a: The student is using mastery experiences (past performance accomplishments) — the most powerful source of self-efficacy because it provides direct, authentic evidence of one's capability. Vicarious experiences (observing others), verbal persuasion, and physiological states are the other three sources. A wrong answer that cites "verbal persuasion" or "seeing others speak well" reveals inability to distinguish between the four sources and misunderstanding of why direct success experiences are most influential.

questions.q: Priya wants to stop procrastinating on her CUET preparation. She decides to: (a) record her study hours daily in a journal, (b) tell herself "Start with just 10 minutes" when she feels resistance, and (c) treat herself to a favourite snack after completing a 2-hour session. Map each strategy to the correct self-regulation technique (self-observation, self-instruction, self-reinforcement) and explain the psychological mechanism of each.
questions.a: (a) Recording study hours = self-observation (provides objective data to modify behavior). (b) "Start with just 10 minutes" = self-instruction (cognitive restructuring to overcome initiation barrier). (c) Snack after 2 hours = self-reinforcement (positive consequence strengthens the target behavior). A wrong mapping (e.g., calling the snack "self-instruction") reveals confusion between antecedent-focused (instruction) and consequence-focused (reinforcement) techniques.

questions.q: Compare and contrast how Bandura's social learning theory explains the development of self-efficacy versus how Skinner's operant conditioning would explain the same behavior change. Use the example of a child learning to ride a bicycle.
questions.a: Bandura: Child observes others riding (vicarious learning), forms cognitive representation, believes "I can do it" (self-efficacy), then attempts and succeeds — mastery experience strengthens self-efficacy. Skinner: Child's riding behavior is shaped by successive approximations reinforced by praise/parental attention; no cognitive mediation or self-belief construct needed. A wrong answer that equates the two or omits the cognitive mediational processes (observation → expectation → self-efficacy) reveals failure to grasp the social-cognitive vs. behaviorist distinction central to Bandura's theory.

questions.q: Critique the statement: "High self-esteem always leads to high academic achievement." Use research evidence from the NCERT text and the distinction between self-esteem and self-efficacy to justify your position.
questions.a: The statement is false. NCERT states: "children with high academic self-esteem perform better in schools than those with low academic self-esteem" — note the domain-specific qualifier "academic self-esteem," not global self-esteem. Self-efficacy (belief about capability in a specific domain) is a stronger predictor of achievement than global self-esteem. High global self-esteem without domain-specific self-efficacy can lead to unrealistic optimism and poor effort. A wrong answer that agrees with the statement reveals conflation of global self-esteem with domain-specific self-efficacy and ignorance of the directional causality (achievement → self-esteem as much as self-esteem → achievement).

questions.q: Design a 4-week self-regulation intervention for a Class 12 student who wants to reduce social media usage from 4 hours/day to 1 hour/day. Specify how you would incorporate all three techniques (self-observation, self-instruction, self-reinforcement) and include a method to measure progress.
questions.a: Week 1: Self-observation — install screen-time tracker, log daily usage without judgment. Week 2: Add self-instruction — set implementation intention: "When I feel urge to open Instagram, I will take 3 deep breaths and open NCERT instead." Week 3: Add self-reinforcement — reward each day ≤1.5 hrs with 30 min guilt-free leisure; weekly reward for meeting target. Week 4: Fade external rewards, internalize self-praise. Measure: daily screen-time report, weekly average. A poor answer that omits baseline measurement, uses only punishment, or lacks specific self-instruction scripts reveals inability to operationalize abstract techniques into a structured behavior-change plan.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Self-esteem is an ______'s overall subjective evaluation of their own worth and value.
Fill in the blank: Imagine a Class 12 student, Rohan, who wants to score 90% in Psychology but feels anxious about his ______.
What is Self-esteem? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Self-esteem is an individual's overall subjective evaluation of their own worth and value.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) Distinguish between self-esteem (evaluative), self-efficacy (belief about capability), and self-regulation (process of control) with concrete examples; (2) Explain how Bandura's social learning theory (observational learning, modelling) forms the basis of self-efficacy development; (3) Apply the three.
